sections.heading: What I do
body: Mostly product design for web, mobile and desktop. I also design websites and design systems, and build prototypes people can click through and use.

sections.heading: Right now
body: UI/UX designer at AmaliTech, based in Takoradi, Ghana. I design in Figma and build a working prototype when a static mockup won't answer the question.

sections.heading: How I work
body: I like time to understand a problem before I start designing. Rushing to a deadline usually means solving the wrong thing.
I ask questions early and share work while it's still rough. It's faster than guessing what people meant.

sections.heading: Parallel interests
body: Photography, and 3D modelling and sculpting in my spare time.

amalitech.title: Rebuilding the AmaliTech website
amalitech.summary: AmaliTech's website ran on a WordPress template that couldn't keep up with the company. I led design on the rebuild as a CMS-backed site, including the design system and the writing guidelines the team now publishes with.

meta.label: Scope
meta.value: Design system, tone of voice, editorial guidelines

highlights: Moved from a WordPress template to a CMS the team manages itself.
Design system, tone of voice and editorial guidelines written from scratch.
Time on site up about 15% after launch.

hero.alt: The rebuilt AmaliTech website home page
hero.caption: The rebuilt home page.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: The site was built on a WordPress template picked early on for speed. Over time, new pages had to fit what the template allowed, brand details drifted from page to page, and most changes beyond text edits needed a developer.

sections.heading: Team and my role
sections.body: Two designers, Gina and me, working with engineering, content, product and marketing. I was the lead designer.
list: Designed the system and the page templates.
Ran user research with Gina and turned the feedback into a list of changes the team could work through.
Set up regular design critiques between the two of us to keep our work consistent.
Reviewed work in progress with engineering and content in alignment meetings.

sections.heading: Process
sections.body: We planned the site as a set of CMS modules the team could combine into pages. I designed the modules and the rules for using them, tested pages with users during the build, and changed modules based on what came back.

sections.heading: Deliverables
list: Design system: type, colour, spacing and components for every page type the company publishes.
Tone of voice for headlines, captions and calls to action.
Editorial guidelines on page structure and what goes where.
CMS templates built from the system's components.

media.alt: The services page: a six-card capability grid built from one card component
media.caption: Services page. All six cards use the same component.

sections.heading: After launch
sections.body: The team builds and publishes pages from the templates without a designer. The insights section gets the most use.

media.alt: The CMS-backed insights index: search, tags, and a card grid of dated articles
media.caption: Insights index, published by the content team.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: Time on site went up about 15% after the new site launched, and new pages no longer wait for design or development time.

media.alt: An engagement-model accordion flowing into a client and partner logo wall
media.caption: Engagement models and the client logo wall.

sections.heading: What I'd change
sections.body: I'd give the component library a named owner and a short review process from the start. Without one, new pages drift from the system as the site grows.

trackpad.title: LazeR, a phone trackpad
trackpad.summary: An Android app and a Windows companion that turn your phone into a trackpad and remote for your laptop. They connect directly over your Wi-Fi, encrypted, after you pair them with a QR code.
highlights: Trackpad gestures, keyboard, media keys, volume, brightness and mic mute from the phone.
QR pairing. Traffic is encrypted and stays on the local network.
Ten releases since August, with in-app updates on the phone and the laptop.

hero.alt: The Android control screen and its settings sheet, recreated from the app
hero.caption: Phone app with media controls, the trackpad and settings.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: I wanted to control my laptop from the sofa. The apps I tried were unreliable or needed setup I had to look up. My phone already has a good touch surface, so I built the remote around the gestures people already use on a laptop trackpad.

sections.heading: Gestures
list: One finger moves the pointer, tap to click. Optional pointer acceleration.
Two fingers scroll in both directions. The app on the laptop decides what that does.
Pinch to zoom.
Three fingers left or right to switch apps.
A keyboard panel, and a shortcuts sheet for copy, paste, undo and redo.

media.alt: The full-bleed trackpad expanded, and the keyboard panel for typing on the laptop
media.caption: Full-screen pad and the keyboard panel.

sections.heading: Releases since July
list: 2.0, August: removed access from outside the home network. The relay needed servers to run, and almost all use is on the same Wi-Fi.
2.1: security fixes and UX polish on both apps.
2.2, September: a landscape layout that docks media and keys beside the pad, and a setting for which side the scroll bar sits on.
2.3: in-app updates for the phone app, after a full audit of both apps.
2.5, November: laptop window redesigned in Material 3 to match the phone.
2.6: mute the laptop's mic from the phone, or use the phone as the laptop's microphone.

sections.heading: Laptop app
sections.body: The laptop side shows the QR code for pairing. It now starts with Windows, updates itself, and recovers from sleep and firewall problems without restarting or re-pairing.

media.alt: LazeR laptop window: a Ready badge, the laptop name and a QR code under 'Connect your phone'
media.caption: Laptop window after the 2.5 redesign.

sections.heading: Audit
sections.body: On 23 September I audited both apps for security, stored data, reliability and UX flows. Every high-priority finding was checked by hand against the code, and the fixes shipped in 2.3.

sections.heading: What I'd change
sections.body: I built the off-network relay in July and removed it in August. I should have shipped the local-network version first and waited to see whether anyone needed remote access.

video-conferencing.title: Video conferencing app
video-conferencing.summary: A video calling web app I designed and built. Most of the design work went into the parts around the call: the lobby, joining, presence and leaving.
highlights: Pre-call lobby with a device check and mic meter.
Every surface built from a few shared components: dialog, sheet, popover, tooltip.

hero.alt: The pre-call lobby: a camera preview, device toggles, and a mic level meter
hero.caption: Pre-call lobby with a device check and live mic meter.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Joining is where most calling tools are weakest. You aren't sure you're in the right room or that your mic works, and it's hard to tell who is actually there. Small actions during a call, like reacting or stepping away, take too many steps.

media.alt: The landing screen: start a new meeting or join one by name or code
media.caption: Start or join from one screen.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body: I built every surface from five shared components: dialog, sheet, popover, tooltip and the call stage. Sign-in is a dialog like everything else, and it's passwordless.

media.alt: The passwordless sign-in dialog: continue with Google, or an email sign-in link
media.caption: Passwordless sign-in in the standard dialog.

sections.heading: Around the call
list: Presence: who is in the call, muted, speaking or away.
Reactions and call sounds.
Picture-in-picture and media-session controls, so the call keeps going when you switch tabs.
Background blur and noise suppression.
Blocks and mutes for moderation.

sections.heading: Accessibility and testing
sections.body: Keyboard navigation throughout, a live region that announces state changes, and automated accessibility checks in CI. Mobile had its own UX pass. End-to-end and capacity tests run against a full room.

media.alt: Appearance settings: theme colour tokens, high-contrast, and vision-assistive colours
media.caption: The theme comes from a few named tokens. High-contrast and vision-assistive modes use the same tokens.

sections.heading: What I'd change
sections.body: It's designed for small calls, and past a dozen people the grid gets hard to read. I'd design large calls as a separate view.

weaver.title: Weaver, an image discovery feed
weaver.summary: A personal discovery feed. It learns my taste from images I've saved, finds new images from open sources, and ranks them against that taste.
highlights: Saved images are used as taste signal and never shown in the feed.
OpenCLIP embeddings in pgvector. New images ranked by distance to my taste clusters.
Runs on free tiers. A daily GitHub Actions job refreshes the pool of new images.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: My Pinterest feed kept showing me more of what I'd already saved, or what was popular. I wanted my saves to be used to find work I hadn't seen.

sections.heading: Version one
sections.body: The first version pulled my saves from different sites into one feed. It worked, but it only showed images I already had. So I changed what each image is for: saves became taste signal and are never shown, and the feed shows new images from open sources ranked against them.

media.alt: The tune-your-taste panel: add an interest, and more/less-like-this concept chips
media.caption: Adjusting the feed in words: more of this, less of that.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: Images are embedded with OpenCLIP. My taste is a few clusters built from my saves. New images are scored by distance to those clusters, with some room left for exploration so the feed doesn't settle on one style. Saving an image updates the clusters.

media.alt: An expanded image with like / not-my-taste controls and a 'threads from this' grid of similar work
media.caption: "Threads from this" shows similar images.

sections.heading: Build
list: PWA, so it installs and runs like an app on a phone.
Supabase and pgvector for storage and search, on free tiers.
A daily GitHub Actions job pulls new candidates from sources including Wikimedia, the Art Institute of Chicago, Reddit, DeviantArt and Tumblr.
Motion respects reduced-motion settings. Semantic markup, focus management, alt text and AA contrast throughout.

media.alt: The Weaver feed on a phone: a two-column masonry with some cards tilted like pinned scraps
media.caption: The feed on a phone.

sections.heading: Changes since launch
list: July: made Weaver public. Anyone can browse as a guest. The library, taste and import screens are only visible to me.
September: thumbnails of new candidates are cached in Weaver's own storage, because images on the source sites get deleted.

sections.heading: What I'd change
sections.body: Ranking by distance to the clusters works, but it's blunt. Weaver already logs which images I engage with, for a learned ranker I parked to get the first version out. Building that ranker is the next step.

booking-room.title: Meeting room booking
booking-room.summary: A meeting room booking system for organisations. You search by time, capacity and amenities, and the database blocks double bookings.
highlights: Search rooms by date, time, capacity and amenities.
Double bookings blocked in the database. Recurring bookings and ICS export.

hero.caption: Dashboard with today's bookings and rooms.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.body: Booking a room meant checking a calendar, guessing a free slot and hoping nobody took it first. The goal was to find a suitable room and hold it in a few steps.

sections.heading: My role
sections.body: Solo design and build, with AI-assisted development.
list: Designed the calendar interactions, the room finder and the conflict rules.
Ran research and feedback rounds with people who book rooms, and changed the flows based on what they said.
Decided the data model and which features to leave out.

sections.heading: Booking
list: Day, week and month calendars. Drag on the calendar to create a booking.
Room finder filtered by date, time, capacity and amenities.
Keyboard shortcuts for booking a room and finding one.
A booking drawer with the details and comments together.

sections.heading: Conflicts and approvals
list: Overlaps are blocked by the database as well as the UI. A meeting ending at 11:00 doesn't block one starting at 11:00.
Recurring bookings, a guard against booking past slots, and ICS export.
Approvers can suggest another time when they turn a request down.
Each booking has a comment thread for the people involved.

sections.heading: Organisation setup
sections.body: Locations, buildings, floors and rooms in one hierarchy, each with its own timezone. Three roles: admin, booking user and view-only. Rooms can require approval, and every change goes to an audit log.

media.alt: Rooms grid with search and filters
media.caption: Rooms list with filters.

sections.heading: Reports
sections.body: Each room shows how often it's booked, when demand peaks and how much of its capacity gets used. The figures roll up to building and organisation level, so facilities teams can see which rooms sit empty.

sections.heading: What I'd change
sections.body: The four-level location hierarchy suits a large organisation and is too much for one office. I'd add a simple mode with one room and one calendar, so a small team never has to open the admin panel.

danmu.title: Danmu, a 3D room planner
danmu.summary: A browser app for planning a room in 3D at its real size. You pick a floor shape or photograph the room, then move, resize and restyle the furniture. There's no account or server, and rooms stay on your device.

meta.label: Stack
meta.value: Next.js · React Three Fiber · TypeScript · on-device ONNX

highlights: Started as an AI makeover app behind an API key. Now a 3D planner you can open in two clicks.
Sizes come from fixed rules for real furniture. If a piece doesn't fit, the app says so.
Rooms are saved in the browser and shared as a file, without the photos.

hero.alt: The Danmu 3D studio: a furnished living room with the catalogue on the left and a details panel on the right
hero.caption: The 3D studio with the starter living room.

sections.heading: Context
sections.body: Room planners tend to be either CAD software, accurate but technical and tied to an account, or mood-board apps where the sizes aren't real. Danmu is for people who rearrange rooms as a hobby and sometimes go on to buy the furniture, so it had to be easy to pick up and accurate enough to buy from.

sections.heading: My role
sections.body: Solo project. AI agents wrote most of the code. I set the direction and reviewed the work.
list: Decided who it's for and what it should never do: no AI image generation, no backend.
Designed the 3D studio, the 2D plan, the photo flow and the copy.
Wrote a one-page brief of product rules that every change was checked against.
Reviewed changes in the browser before they merged, and reversed decisions when testing showed they were wrong.

sections.heading: Version one
sections.body: The June version asked for a Google AI key before showing anything. You took six photos of the room and an image model generated a makeover. It had about 15 screens, a carpenter's cut sheet and share links. The renders looked good, but the sizes couldn't be trusted. The model would happily fit a sofa against a wall too short for it.

sections.heading: 6 June to July: removing the AI renders
sections.body: I removed the key wall first, so a new user lands in a furnished room in two clicks. In July the render pipeline was deleted. AI now does one job, spotting furniture in your photos, and it's optional.

sections.heading: Sizes come from rules
sections.body: Every size goes through fixed limits for real furniture, doors and walls, and AI can only suggest a size. When a piece doesn't fit, the app keeps it at its real size and says why. The room report (walkways, door swings, space around the bed) and the 2D plan use the same rules, so the two views always agree.

media.alt: The 2D floor plan: a 6 by 4 metre room with labelled walls, dimensions and furniture outlines
media.caption: 2D plan of the same room.

sections.heading: 3 October: typical sizes for scanned furniture
sections.body: The plan was to measure furniture from the photos. Testing on real rooms showed the measurements were often wrong: windows came out with deep sills and curtains came out tiny. So I changed it. A piece found in a photo now gets a typical size and colour, the app says so, and you type the real size if you need it.

media.alt: The studio with a prompt reading 'These are typical sizes. Measure your room and type the real width, depth and height.'
media.caption: The prompt shown after a photo scan.

sections.heading: Ideas
sections.body: The first Suggest button rearranged the whole room at once, gave one result and no reason. I replaced it with Ideas, a page of alternative layouts. Each is a small plan with a caption like "Sofa against the front wall, facing the TV · 5 pieces move". There's no score. Tapping an idea applies it in 3D, "Back to your room" undoes it, and pinned pieces stay where they are.

media.alt: The Ideas gallery: four mini floor plans, each captioned with what moves, beside the 3D room
media.caption: Ideas panel, four layouts per page.

sections.heading: Privacy
list: No server or account. Rooms are stored in the browser, and the app works offline after the first visit.
To share a room you save a file and send it. The file has the room and furniture but no photos.
Furniture detection runs on the device. Adding a second detection model raised the hits on a test room from 7 to 13 of 19 pieces.

sections.heading: First screen
sections.body: The first screen used to be a hero illustration above three identical cards. I replaced it with a drawing sheet: three numbered ways to start, and a scaled plan of the starter room drawn from the same data the app opens.

media.alt: Danmu's first screen: 'Your room, drawn to scale' with three numbered ways in beside a dimensioned floor plan
media.caption: First screen.

sections.heading: How the work was run
list: A one-page brief with ten product rules. A rule went in only after breaking it had cost real work.
Decisions logged with dates, including the ones we decided against.
A visual-check list for things only a person in a browser can judge, plus audits of the 2D plan, mobile and the whole platform.
Standing help text removed across the app. Warnings, privacy notes and explanations of why something can't be done stayed.

sections.heading: What I'd change
sections.body: I'd design the phone layout earlier. The mobile audit came in September, after the studio had been built around a laptop screen with two side panels, and a lot of later work went into retrofitting it.
